violated_invariant: Tokens may only be pulled from `from` if `from` actually authorized the router (via a real permit or its own call); a no-op permit on an attacker-supplied token's underlying must not authorize transferFrom of a third party's approval.
notes: The router takes an attacker-chosen `token`, reads its underlying (WETH), calls permit on it, and then transferFrom(from, ...) using whatever allowance `from` had already granted the router; WETH has no permit, its fallback swallows the call, so the signature is never checked. Finding 0 (arbitrary-send-erc20-permit) names exactly this: an arbitrary `from` in transferFrom combined with a permit call in anySwapOutUnderlyingWithPermit, the exploited function, so it qualifies. Findings 1 and 2 flag the same pattern in the two sibling functions that were not used but share the weakness.

violated_invariant: A swap must never decrease the stable-pool invariant D beyond fees; rounding in balance upscaling and in the amount-out path must favor the pool, not the trader, even when a balance has been pushed to a few wei.
notes: The attacker uses batch swaps to drive one token balance down to a handful of wei, where the round-down in _upscale/_swapGivenOut (balances and amountOut scaled with mulDown) makes the computed invariant D drop relative to real balances, so BPT and the other tokens can be bought cheaply and the pool unwound at a profit. No Slither finding touches StableMath, BaseGeneralPool or the scaling helpers; the 44 divide-before-multiply hits are all in the LogExpMath library, which is unrelated to the stable invariant path, so nothing explains the exploit. The uninitialized-local and unused-return hits on the pool contracts are deliberate patterns, so I marked them invalid; the rest are left unresolved. The two pool candidates share the same source, so the same indices apply to both.

violated_invariant: The vault's USDC-to-WETH conversion must execute at a fair price (minimum-out / TWAP), and must not be triggerable by an arbitrary caller who has just moved the spot price of the pool it swaps through.
notes: The PoC flash-loans USDC, skews the USDC/WETH V3 pool, calls the permissionless vault.swapToWETH(100k USDC) which swaps at the manipulated price with no slippage floor, then reverses the pool and keeps the difference. The vault contract 0x6a06... has no recovered source (sourcify not_found) and the only candidates with Slither output are third-party contracts (Morpho, OKX DexRouter, TokenApprove, the Uniswap pool) that are not the defect, so there is nothing to adjudicate; the function name comes from the PoC interface, not verified source.

violated_invariant: An authorized signature must bind every field that determines what the strategy will approve and call (fromToken, toToken, amount, aggregator), not only the calldata bytes.
notes: _validateAuthorization hashes only keccak256(swap.data) for each SwapInfo, so the signer's approval does not cover fromToken/toToken/amount/aggregator; the attacker reuses a valid signature with aggregator set to their own contract and amount = max, and executeSwap then forceApproves the gauge token to that aggregator and calls it. Slither has no detector for incomplete EIP-712 coverage; the reentrancy-balance hits (99-102) on executeSwap flag the external call but describe reentrancy, not the missing signature binding, so none explains. The timestamp and uninitialized-local hits at the defect function are noise (a deadline comparison and a bytes variable that is appended to).

violated_invariant: The router may only transferFrom the account that initiated the current lock; the payer in payCallback must be derived from the caller, not from attacker-supplied payload data.
notes: The exploited contract is the Ekubo EVM router (0x8ccb...), whose payCallback accepted a payer address from the lock payload and called transferFrom on it, so any address with a standing WBTC approval to the router could be drained by looping core.lock (85 times, 0.2 WBTC each). The router has no recovered source, and the PoC replaces it with a readable stand-in, so the function names are reconstructed; Ekubo Core (which has source) only forwards lock/pay callbacks and is not the defect, so I did not adjudicate its findings.

violated_invariant: A rollup proof accepted by escapeHatch must cryptographically bind the withdrawals paid out by processDepositsAndWithdrawals to valid, previously deposited notes; value cannot leave the rollup except for what the circuit constrains.
notes: The permissionless escapeHatch forwards a caller-built proof to the external TurboVerifier (0x48cb..., not a candidate) with rollupSize taken from the proof; the verifier accepted a proof whose public withdrawal inputs were not bound by the deployed escape-hatch verification key, and the processor then paid out the rollup's ETH/DAI/renBTC to the attacker. The defect is in the proof system / verifier key and the processor's trust of proof-decoded outputs, which no Slither detector can model; the arbitrary-send-eth and reentrancy hits on withdraw describe the payout mechanics, not the broken validation, so none explains. Confidence is low because the real flaw lives outside the recovered Solidity.

violated_invariant: The factory must only issue initializePool/mint calls to the PositionManager on behalf of the new launch; caller-supplied calldata executed with the factory as msg.sender must not be able to change approvals or touch other launches' positions.
notes: launch() is permissionless and passes initCalldata and modifyCalldata verbatim into PositionManager.multicall with the factory as msg.sender, so the attacker substituted setApprovalForAll(attacker, true) and then burned every factory-owned LP position. Slither reports unused-return (53) and reentrancy-benign on that exact multicall line, but those describe ignoring a return value / event ordering, not the forwarding of unvalidated calldata to an external contract, so none explains; the arbitrary-send-eth hit is the intended dust refund to msg.sender. The unchecked-transfer hits are genuine (raw transfer on arbitrary paired tokens), the uninitialized-local hits are accumulators intentionally starting at zero.

violated_invariant: A registry's initialize() must be callable once, by the deployer only; the manager that controls which implementation item-adapter clones delegatecall into must not be replaceable by an arbitrary caller.
notes: Both live contract registries exposed an unprotected initialize(uint256) that re-set the pending manager, so the attacker re-ran it, accepted manager, registered their own code as the body for the item adapters' transfer selectors, pulled 54 items from holders without approval and melted them for ENJ. Neither registry nor the platform has recovered source (only the ENJ token, which is not the defect), so function names are taken from the PoC interface and there are no Slither findings to adjudicate.

violated_invariant: transfer(to, x) called by a counterparty that means 'x wei' must move x wei; a token whose transfer silently re-interprets small values as NFT ids and moves a full unit breaks the accounting of any AMM holding it.
notes: O404.transfer treats any valueOrId <= maxTotalSupplyERC721 (50) as an NFT id and moves a full 1e18 units plus the NFT; a Uniswap V3 exact-output swap for `id` wei makes the pool call transfer(attacker, id) and hand over 1e18 O404 while only debiting a few wei, after the attacker arranged (via pool.flash repaid by id-path transfers) for the pool to own the low ids. Slither's erc721-interface hits (7-10) complain that approve/transferFrom return bool, which is the ERC-404 hybrid by design and says nothing about the id/amount overloading, so none explains and I marked them invalid. The dual interpretation is inherent ERC-404 v1 design, but it is a code-level logic flaw when the token whitelists an AMM pool, so it stays in scope.

violated_invariant: Interest for an idle period must be accrued once, at the utilization that held during that period; a depositor who arrives after the gap must not earn the whole gap's deposit interest at a utilization they set in the same block.
notes: _checkFirstAction stores the full 264k-block idle gap as inactiveActionDelta and freezes actionEXR on the block's first action, and the interest model (0x29ec..., not a candidate) then multiplies that whole gap by a rate computed from live totals on every later action in the block, so a flash-loaned deposit plus borrows to spike utilization credits ~36 days of interest that a repay/withdraw loop cashes out. Slither's unused-return hits (70, 85) sit on the exact setBlocks/syncActionEXR lines but only say a bool return is ignored, not that the gap is applied at manipulable utilization, so none explains. The proxy's controlled-delegatecall hits are false positives (fixed handler address and fixed selectors) and the reentrancy-balance hits on the ERC20 wrappers are noise. The logic contract 0x47be... is the handler the proxy delegates to; the proxy itself only forwards.
